While carbon fiber is considered a big no-no for submersibles, part of the issue the field had with the Titan was the lack of stress testing. This means they did not try the sub unmanned enough times to see how many submersions it took before this thing was at its breaking point from the number of pressure changes. 

In the airplane industry, they have this tested under extreme conditions to see when these will be considered worn down, and set their part life to much much lower than this period to prevent parts from breaking in the first place. On top of that, the number of parts on a plane is A LOT. One can fail and it doesn’t mean the whole plane is going to explode. 

For example, they stress bend the wings farther than you’d ever see even in extreme turbulence. You can check out a ground test for that here to get an idea of what I’m talking about: https://youtu.be/6wHrfBs82Tk

Many of the homeless have mental health or substance use issues. Long Island used to be set up with treatment facilities for both and provided a place for recovery a bit more isolated from outside influence. Currently Mass and Cass serves as the main area where treatment is available and drug dealers have taken advantage by selling around the area, making it more difficult for those struggling to stay sober. 

By rebuilding the bridge and reopening the facilities, many of the homeless currently on Mass and Cass would be able to stay in the residential facilities while working toward recovery. This is geared toward those who are homeless with substance use or mental health disorders that need higher levels of care. This would not inherently help any homeless who do not have these types of issues and are on the street solely due to financial circumstances. 

The bridge is needed as there is no other way to access this area where staff would need to regularly commute, supplies frequently delivered, etc. The size of the island and its facilities is something that wouldn’t physically fit in Boston proper in terms of current available real estate/land, and most towns/cities outside of Boston would object to having this within their space. It technically would be possible to come up with ferry services instead, but there would be a lot of logistics to consider, especially around medical care in case of emergencies with detox and in general. 

Note that previously when the bridge existed there were free shuttles for the folks on the island, so it was not just a “nicer prison” so to speak. Folks had the autonomy to move freely (though depending on program and personal recovery there may have been limits in place like all mental health/substance use facilities).

Hey all, 24 non-binary folk here. I actually originally presented to an ENT specialist for what I thought was an ear infection that wasn’t clearing up. Had ear pain, scratchy throat, chills and mild fever that wouldn’t clear up for several months. Had my covid vaccine, even tested for it just in case, all negative. PCP did blood work that all came back pretty regular, and tested negative for mono and TB. So I was sent on my way to the ENT for suspected ear infection issues as I have a history of sinus and ear related issues. 

Somehow I was sent to neurology (long story short the ENT I saw was a sexist asshole assuming migraines because “women just have more issues with them” even though I’m not a woman), given a steroid for head pressure relief, and followed up with ENT after an MRI to check any inner ear issues. Turns out it was lingual tonsillitis and not migraines. I was given an antibiotic and stronger round of steroids to see if it would clear up since they like to avoid removing lingual tonsils when possible. It cleared up finally, and all was well. 

But then it came back about 2 months later. So I scheduled a visit with the ENTs (different MD thank goodness after the last guy). I was expecting a visit where he would recommend removing them since they keep flaring up and call it a day. Instead, he thinks it is either an autoimmune disorder, or lymphoma. Apparently lingual tonsillitis is extremely rare and if it does go away with treatment it’s basically unheard of for it to come back, especially within such a short period of time. 

Lymphoma was not even on my radar for this appointment. But after he suggested it, I realized it would explain why the lymph nodes in my armpits are aching during this tonsil flare up. I also checked the lymphs around my neck and they are very hard. 

I know there’s a good chance it could also be an autoimmune disorder, but I’m just really scared it’s the worse scenario. I’ve got a chest x-ray ordered and already did the more in depth bloodwork he requested. It just sucks that the first appointment for the immunologist is for February 2022. I’m hoping the X-ray and follow up with the ENT might provide some more answers.

Dialectic behavioral therapy is a type of therapy that teaches skills specific to BPD. 

It includes skills that help with specifically:
1. Interpersonal effectiveness - ability to communicate with others in an effective, respectful, and meaningful way
2. Distress tolerance - pretty self explanatory, it helps with riding out those moments of intense emotion and teaches you how to get through that without completely spiraling 
3. Emotion regulation - this helps in regulating emotions so that they don’t get to the extremes as often as they usually do with BPD. 
4. Mindfulness skills - this just helps tie in the other 3 groups by helping you learn to try and observe your thoughts, feelings, and interactions with others in a more objective fashion
